content: I started with a question from a class project that I could not answer with the examples in our textbook. My advisor helped me narrow it into one measurable problem, and I spent the first week reading papers before writing any code. Keeping a small experiment log saved me when an early result turned out to be caused by a data split mistake. I wrote the methods section while the experiments were fresh, then revised the introduction after I understood what the results actually supported. Submitting the paper was nerve-racking, but the process taught me that clear limitations are just as important as promising results.
summary: A practical account of moving from a class project to a first research paper.
title: How I wrote my first research paper

content: In my third year, every interesting topic seemed either too broad or too advanced to begin. I made a shortlist by looking for questions that appeared repeatedly in recent papers but still had a small, testable gap. Talking with faculty and senior students helped me check whether the data and tools were realistically available. I also picked a topic where a useful negative result would still teach me something, rather than relying on one ideal outcome. A focused question gave me a better starting point than trying to choose the most fashionable area.
summary: A way to find a focused research question that fits your time and experience.
title: Choosing a research topic as a third-year student

content: When I review a paper, I first try to identify the exact claim the authors want readers to believe. I then check whether the methods and comparisons provide enough evidence for that claim, rather than expecting every paper to solve an entire field. Clear descriptions of datasets, baselines, and limitations make it much easier to assess the contribution fairly. I value a well-supported modest result more than a sweeping conclusion built on a narrow experiment. My most useful reviews explain the reasoning behind each concern and suggest a practical way to address it.
summary: Reviewing is about evaluating a paper's evidence and helping its authors improve.
title: What I look for as a reviewer

content: I first tried LaTeX the night before a report was due and spent more time fixing braces than checking my argument. The turning point was moving the paper into small files and compiling after each meaningful change. I learned to keep figures and bibliography entries in predictable folders, and to read the first error in the log instead of guessing at the last one. Version control also made collaboration calmer because we could review changes instead of passing around renamed document copies. I still look up commands, but the workflow now feels dependable rather than mysterious.
summary: Small habits that made writing and collaborating in LaTeX less frustrating.
title: Learning LaTeX the hard way

content: Our course project became a possible paper only after we stopped treating the demo as the main contribution. We revisited the project question, added a baseline, and repeated the evaluation on data that had not guided our design choices. A faculty mentor helped us separate what we had actually measured from what we had hoped the system would do. We also documented setup steps so another student could reproduce the central result without our laptops. The extra work took longer than the original course, but it gave us a much clearer and more honest story to submit.
summary: How a course project can become a stronger research submission with careful follow-up.
title: Turning a course project into a conference paper
